_readme: All example content for the Coming soon page lives here. Edit numbers, sources and wording in this file; the page code does not need to change. Every figure is graded by a model on a small sample, not by a lawyer. Names are shown as they appear in the published decisions (Daniel, 2026-10-13); no masking is needed for examples from published decisions.

layers_intro.title: Three layers on a decision, one tap away
layers_intro.text: The decision text stays the page. Three optional layers sit on top of it, each opened with a button: a summary of the case, a map of the questions the court decided, and one plain sentence on what each paragraph does. Try the buttons below.
layers_intro.limits: These are real stored outputs for decisions from the hand-picked set of 150 important Federal Court immigration decisions. Names are as published in the decisions; paragraph text is shortened. It is a picture of the feature, not the working reader.

cases.level: Visa agent form-letter refusal, then Federal Court
cases.subject: Whether a visa agent's unexplained form-letter refusal of a Federal Skilled Worker application (NOC 7372 duties under s.75(2) Regulations) was reasonable and adequately reasoned, and whether an agent's later affidavit can supply the reasons.

args.text: The agent's affidavit explains the reasoning: the applicant's evidence showed experience in only two of the listed main duties.
Under Newfoundland Nurses the court may fill evidentiary lacunae and draw logical inferences from the record to uphold the decision, even where reasons are thin.

cases.outcome: Judicial review granted; agent's decision set aside and referred back to CIC for reconsideration by a different agent

issues.q: Whether the decision maker's affidavit can serve as valid reasons for the decision in lieu of contemporaneous notes.
Whether the decision maker provided sufficient reasons to allow for meaningful judicial review of the eligibility determination.
issues.quote: It is entirely unclear why the decision was reached.

notes: The applicant applied for permanent residence under the Federal Skilled Worker class based on experience under NOC 7372, driller and blaster.

The applicant applied for permanent residence in Canada under the Federal Skilled Worker (FSW) class on the basis of his stated experience under national occupational classification code (NOC) 7372, driller and blaster. He has a bachelor’s degree in geology and a certificate in blasting from the Ministry of Mines and Steel Development in Nigeria. He is employed as a quarry supe…

Subsection 75(2) of the Regulations describes a skilled worker as a foreign national who performed the tasks in the NOC lead statement and a substantial number of the main duties, including all essential duties.

Subsection 75(2) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, SOR/2002-227 (Regulations) describes a skilled worker as, inter alia, a foreign national who has performed the tasks described in the lead statement for the occupation as set out in the NOC occupational descriptions and performed a substantial number of the main duties of the occupation, including all “esse…
The officer determined the applicant did not provide evidence satisfying the requirement and was not eligible for further processing under subsection 75(3) of the Regulations.

A Citizenship and Immigration Canada agent determined that the applicant did not provide evidence that he satisfied this requirement and was not eligible for further processing pursuant to subsection 75(3) of the Regulations.

The decision was a form letter stating the agent was not satisfied the applicant performed the lead statement actions or substantial main duties, and the agent later swore an affidavit claiming the evidence showed experience in only two main duties.

The decision is a form letter which states that the agent was not satisfied that the applicant had performed the actions in the lead statement for the occupation or a substantial number of the main duties. The agent subsequently swore an affidavit for this judicial review stating that the applicant’s evidence only demonstrated experience in two of the listed main duties.
The Court states decision makers may not supplement reasons by affidavit but may explain contemporaneous notes, citing Taleb v Canada.

Decision makers may not supplement their reasons by way of an affidavit, but they may provide an explanation for their notes made contemporaneous to the decision: Taleb v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2012 FC 384, paras 24-25.
The Court finds the affidavit inadmissible because it lacks contemporaneous notes, was sworn months after the decision, and goes beyond explaining notes by tendering reasons.

In this case, the agent has no contemporaneous notes which describe her reasoning process. The affidavit was sworn on July 30, 2012, three months after the decision, casting doubt as to its reliability. It necessarily goes beyond explaining the agent’s notes, as there are none, and is tendered as reasons for the decision. The affidavit is therefore inadmissible.

The applicant's employer letter stated the applicant schedules drilling, maps holes, decides when to suspend or continue drilling, calculates explosives, supervises subordinates, ensures safety, and connects blasting circuits.

The applicant’s employer provided a letter stating that, among other things, he: (a) schedules, supervises and coordinates drilling operations, (b) maps the pattern of holes and determines their size and spacing, (c) decides when to suspend or continue drilling, (d) calculates the amount of explosives required, (e) supervises subordinates in carrying out charging operations, (g…
The Court holds it cannot determine if the applicant performed the NOC duties; the agent must provide reasoning, as without it, assessing reasonableness is impossible per Gulati.

The NOC occupational description states that, “Blasters in this group fill blast holes with explosives and detonate explosives.” There are six main duties listed, several of which could arguably correspond with the tasks described in the applicant’s evidence, particularly (b) (e) (g) and (h) noted above. It is not for this Court to determine whether the applicant has in fact pe…
The Court finds the decision provides no insight into the agent's reasoning process, as the agent merely stated her conclusion without explanation.
The decision provides no insight into the agent’s reasoning process. The agent merely stated her conclusion, without explanation. It is entirely unclear why the decision was reached.
The Court states Newfoundland Nurses focuses on the outcome, allowing evidentiary lacunae to be filled by the record and logical inferences to uphold the decision.

Newfoundland and Labrador Nurses' Union v Newfoundland and Labrador (Treasury Board), 2011 SCC 62, [2011] 3 SCR 708 does not save the decision. Newfoundland Nurses ensures that the focus of judicial review remains on the outcome or decision itself, and not the process by which that outcome was reached. Where readily apparent, evidentiary lacunae may be filled in when supported …

The Court holds that Newfoundland Nurses does not allow the Court to supply reasons or make findings where the decision is silent on critical issues, and grants the application to set aside the agent's decision.

Newfoundland Nurses is not an open invitation to the Court to provide reasons that were not given, nor is it licence to guess what findings might have been made or to speculate as to what the tribunal might have been thinking. This is particularly so where the reasons are silent on a critical issue. It is ironic that Newfoundland Nurses, a case which at its core is about defere…

cases.level: Refugee Protection Division, then Federal Court
cases.subject: Whether the RPD wrongly treated approaching Mexican police as a legal precondition to state protection, and whether its state protection analysis was adequately reasoned

args.text: The RPD applied the wrong legal test by making approaching the state a legal pre-condition to a finding that state protection is unavailable, without first considering whether it was reasonable not to approach it.
The RPD failed to analyse the evidence on the applicants' personal experiences with police and on similarly situated persons, and gave inadequate reasons, which also breaches procedural fairness.
Current documentary evidence shows that Mexican police, prosecutors and courts are inadequate, rebutting the persuasive decision's state protection finding.
The alleged error is not an error of law but a question of applying the law to the facts, which the respondent disputes.

cases.outcome: application granted; decision set aside and s 97 claim remitted for full reconsideration by a different panel; no question certified

issues.q: Whether the RPD erred in law by treating seeking state protection as a mandatory precondition rather than assessing if it was reasonable for applicants not to seek it.
issues.quote: If instead it believed... that this was a legal pre-condition applicable in all cases, it made an error of law and the decision should be quashed.

issues.q: Whether the RPD's finding that it was unreasonable for applicants not to seek protection was reasonable given their evidence.
issues.quote: In light of the above, the Court concludes that the decision cannot withstand a probing examination and is unreasonable.

notes: The applicant seeks judicial review of the RPD's rejection of their claim because the RPD found the adult applicants had an obligation to approach the state for protection and it was objectively reasonable to have sought it.

the applicant, his wifethe applicant and their two minor daughtersthe applicant andthe applicant are Mexican nationals. They seek judicial review of the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting their claim pursuant to section 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c. 27 (the Act) because the adult applicants "had an obligation to approac…
The RPD found the adult applicants' testimony credible and accepted that the principal applicant was subject to harassment, threats and a kidnapping.

The credibility of the adult applicants is not in dispute here. The RPD specifically found their testimony credible and trustworthy. It accepted that the applicant, a doctor, had been the subject of harassment, threats and a kidnapping orchestrated by the father of a newborn infant who had died after being administered two routine vaccines by the applicant at a rural clinic.
The RPD acknowledged the applicants made serious but unsuccessful attempts to find an internal flight alternative by relocating to three states.

The RPD also acknowledged that the applicants had made serious but ultimately unsuccessful attempts at finding an internal flight alternative, having relocated to three separate states in Mexico, namely Durango, Veracruz and Yucatan.

The applicants submitted they did not seek police protection because they believed it would be ineffective, citing evidence that 70% of kidnappings involve police and their own failed past attempts to obtain assistance.

The applicants readily admitted in their Personal Information Forms (PIF) that they had not sought the protection of the Mexican police, because they both believed that doing so would not afford them any protection. They provided various explanations in their PIFs and at the hearing to justify their position. They also referred to documentary evidence which, according to them, …

The applicants submitted evidence that the state's inability to protect them is a broader pattern, noting that only 1 in 4 or 5 crimes are reported, fewer than 5% are investigated, and fewer than 2% go to trial.

The applicants also put forth evidence to establish that their lack of faith in the ability of the police to protect them relates to a broader pattern, that is, their state's inability to extend its protection. In that respect, they produced documentary evidence indicating that the majority of the population has no faith in the state’s enforcement institutions (police and court…
The applicants pointed to documentary evidence about similarly situated people as proof of the state's inability to protect them from further kidnapping and violence.

The applicants also pointed to documentary evidence relating to similarly situated people, as evidence of the inability of the state to protect them from further kidnapping and violence at the hands of their persecutor.

The applicants claim they established the inadequacy of Mexican enforcement institutions through current evidence, rebutting the RPD's reliance on the 2006 "persuasive decision" and citing the Supreme Court President's statement on the crisis in the penal system and 90 per cent impunity.

Finally, as the RPD had indicated its reliance on the so-called "persuasive decision" issued in TA4-18833 in February 2006, the applicants claim that they have established, through more current documentary evidence, the inadequacy of Mexican enforcement institutions (police, attorneys general and courts) as of the present time. According to the applicants, their evidence rebuts…
The applicants argue the RPD applied the wrong legal test by elevating a requirement to approach the state into a pre-condition without first considering whether it was reasonable not to do so.

Before reviewing in detail the decision of the RPD, it is important to identify the issues raised by the applicants. First, they say that the RPD applied the wrong legal test, more particularly that it elevated to the level of a legal pre-condition that an applicant must actually approach the state to request protection before the RPD can make a finding that state protection is…
The applicants argue the RPD failed to adequately analyze the evidence or provide reasoning for finding it unreasonable not to seek protection, breaching procedural fairness.

Second, the applicants argue that the RPD failed to make an adequate analysis of the evidence before it (particularly with respect to their personal experiences with the police and those of similarly situated persons), or failed to provide adequate reasoning for its finding that it was unreasonable, in this particular case, for the applicants not to seek protection before leavi…
The standard of review is correctness for errors of law but reasonableness for the RPD's finding on state protection availability, unless inadequate reasons breach procedural fairness.

There is no dispute as to the standard of review applicable to all such issues. If indeed there was an error of law (the respondent objects to this characterization of the alleged error) the standard is correctness. However, the finding of the RPD on the availability of state protection, including whether it was unreasonable for the applicants not to have sought such protection…
The Court will now review the decision itself.
With those issues in mind, the Court will now review the decision itself.

The RPD barely discussed the evidence supporting its conclusions, instead adopting the general test from the persuasive decision and stating it was reasonable to assume protection might have been adequate if the claimant had made reasonable efforts.

In contrast to many of its decisions on state protection, in this case the RPD barely discusses the evidence actually supporting its conclusions. Instead, having adopted the general test applied in the persuasive decision referred to above (the adequacy of which is not disputed), it states at paragraph 22: I have taken into consideration that the persuasive decision states that…

The Court discusses the persuasive decision, where the RPD found the applicant did not rebut the presumption of state protection by relying on the Mexican government's anti-narcotic efforts and the applicant's past cooperation with police.

At this stage, the Court must open a parenthesis and discuss in more detail what the persuasive decision was about. It dealt with a claimant allegedly facing persecution (he was not found credible) for having helped the police bust a drug operation. The claimant argued he had rebutted the presumption of state protection, as he had actually sought protection from a local police …
The RPD relied on Kadenko, finding no objective evidence beyond a failed attempt to seek protection to defeat the presumption of state protection.

Apart from his alleged attempt to seek protection from a local police officer, there is no indication in that decision that the claimant had put forth other objective evidence to defeat the presumption of state protection. The situation was thus very similar to that at issue in Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration v. Kadenko (1996), 143 D.L.R. (4th) 532 (F.C.A.), in …

The decision-maker quoted passages from Avila without comment, presumably to show the RPD knew corruption diminishes democracy and required analysis of evidence regarding the applicant as a victim of criminality.

Returning to the case at bar, having adopted the assumption made by the RPD in the persuasive decision (see paragraph 12 above), the decision-maker goes on to quote, without comment, several passages of documentary evidence relied upon by the applicants, including certain extracts from the decision of a Federal Court judge in Avila v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigra…
The RPD noted the applicants' argument that objective documents rebutted the persuasive decision but reverted to its main concern: the applicants' failure to seek protection before departing.

After noting the applicants' argument that "the objective country documents in the decision in [Avila] rebutted the [RPD] persuasive decision TA-4-18833," and that said documents establish that state protection was not available to them, the RPD reverts to the main concern it described at the beginning of its decision, namely, the applicants’ failure to seek protection before d…
The RPD found the claimants had an obligation to seek state protection despite their subjective fears, noting they had detailed information to give the police.

The RPD does not engage in a discussion of the applicants’ personal experiences with the police, or the evidence of similarly situated persons described in the objective country documents with reference to the objective basis for the applicants’ refusal or unwillingness to seek protection. Instead, it notes that the death of the applicant's father supports the applica…
The Court finds it unclear whether the RPD made an error of law or an error in applying the law to the facts.
Looking at the decision as a whole, it is not clear whether the RPD actually made an error of law as opposed to an error in its application of the law to the facts of this case.

The applicants had the burden of establishing on a balance of probabilities that they met the requirements of para. 97(1)(b) of the Act, including being unable or unwilling to avail themselves of their country's protection.

To claim the status of a person in need of protection, the applicants clearly had the burden of establishing, on a balance of probabilities, that they met the requirements set out in para. 97(1)(b) of the Act. Pursuant to subparagraph 97(1)(b)(i), the person must be unable or, because of the risk, unwilling to avail themselves of the protection of their country of origin.
The Court notes that Mexico is a democracy where a presumption of state protection applies, requiring credible evidence to displace it.

Mexico is a democracy to which a presumption of state protection applies, even if its place on the "democracy spectrum" needs to be assessed to determine what credible and reliable evidence will be sufficient to displace that presumption (Hinzman, above, para. 45; Carrillo v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [2007] F.C.J. No. 439, para.19; Avila, above, para. 3…

The Court notes that in developed democracies, rebutting the presumption of state protection requires proof of exhausted recourses and that seeking state protection before Canada is not unreasonable except in exceptional circumstances.

In developed democracies such as the U.S. and Israel, it is clear from Hinzman (at paras. 46 and 57) that to rebut the presumption of state protection, this evidence must include proof that an applicant has exhausted all recourses available to her or him. It is also clear that, except in exceptional circumstances, it would be unreasonable in such countries not to seek state pro…
The Court finds Hinzman does not relieve decision-makers of assessing evidence of state inability to protect in Mexico, noting Ward and Avila.

The Court does not understand Hinzman to say that this conclusion applies to all countries wherever they stand on the "democracy spectrum" and to relieve the decision-maker of his or her obligation to assess the evidence offered to establish that, in Mexico for example, the state is unable (although willing) to protect its citizens, or that it was reasonable for the claimant to…

The Court cannot discern whether the RPD required seeking protection because it viewed Mexico as a developed democracy, believed the obligation applies equally in all cases, or found it unreasonable not to seek protection in this case.

In the present instance, having read the decision under review several times, the Court is unable to discern whether the RPD repeatedly refers to the applicants' obligation to seek protection because: (i) it had assessed that Mexico was a developed democracy similar to the U.S. and Israel; or (ii) whether it believed that such obligation is to apply equally in all cases; or (ii…
The Court finds that if the RPD meant Mexico was a developed democracy, it failed to provide cogent reasoning supporting that implicit conclusion.
If the RPD meant (i), on the basis of the evidence cited in its decision, it certainly failed to provide cogent reasoning supporting this implicit conclusion.
The Court finds that if the RPD believed seeking protection was a legal pre-condition applicable in all cases, it made an error of law and the decision should be quashed.
If instead it believed, as argued by the applicants, that this was a legal pre-condition applicable in all cases, it made an error of law and the decision should be quashed.

The Court finds the RPD's finding flawed because it relied on a distinguishable prior decision, made an unsupported material finding, and raised doubt about its assessment of the applicants' personal experience.

Finally, if in spite of the way the decision actually reads, the RPD concluded as it did solely because it found that it was unreasonable for the applicants, in their particular circumstances, not to seek state protection, this last finding is flawed for the following reasons: a) There is no indication that the RPD made an independent review of the documentary evidence supporti…
The Court concludes the decision is unreasonable, stressing that applicants bear a heavy burden under section 97 of the Act.

In light of the above, the Court concludes that the decision cannot withstand a probing examination and is unreasonable. State protection is a difficult and complex issue and the Court did not come to this conclusion lightly. Again, it is important to stress the fact that the applicants bear a heavy burden here, particularly under section 97 of the Act, and that my decision sho…
The Court grants the application, sets aside the decision, and remits the claim for full reconsideration by a different panel.

Both sides agreed that in the particular circumstances of this case there is no question of general interest to certify. Indeed, the matter turns on its own facts. However, further clarification as to the burden of proof incumbent on claimants with respect to the issue of state protection will be welcome when the Federal Court of Appeal answers the question certified in Carrill…

cases.level: Citizenship Judge, then Federal Court appeal
cases.subject: Moroccan permanent resident denied citizenship for failing to prove physical presence in Canada during the four-year reference period

args.text: The Citizenship Judge erred in computing the days of absence, which was a calculation error (160 days reported for a period of 140 days) that the application shows on its face.
The Judge erred by relying solely on the citizenship application form (391 days absent) and not taking into account the residence questionnaire (351 days) and the corrections the applicant made.

cases.outcome: appeal under s. 14(5) Citizenship Act dismissed

issues.q: Whether the Citizenship Judge erred in denying citizenship because he failed to take into account corrections made by the applicant to his residence questionnaire regarding days of absence.
issues.quote: Given the evidence in the record, I therefore find that the Citizenship Judge did not err and could reasonably conclude that the applicant did not meet the residence requirements.

notes: The applicant appeals under subsection 14(5) of the Citizenship Act, arguing the Citizenship Judge erred in computing days of absence and ignored corrections to the application form.

The applicant is appealing under subsection 14(5) of the Citizenship Act (R.S. 1985, c. C‑29) from the decision of a Citizenship Judge, dated September 9, 2008, denying his application for citizenship. In support of his appeal, the applicant argues essentially that the Citizenship Judge erred by incorrectly computing his days of absence from Canada during the ref…
The Court concludes the application for judicial review must be dismissed after examining the record and submissions.

Having carefully examined the record that was before the Citizenship Judge and the written and oral submissions of the two parties, I have come to the conclusion that this application for judicial review must be dismissed. My reasons are set out in the paragraphs that follow.
The applicant is a citizen of Morocco who arrived in Canada with his wife and three daughters in 1999, obtained permanent resident status in 2000, and whose family was granted citizenship in 2005.

The applicant is a citizen of Morocco. He arrived in Canada with his wife and three daughters on July 23, 1999. He obtained permanent resident status on July 1, 2000. His wife and his three daughters were granted Canadian citizenship in December 2005.
The applicant reported being outside Canada for 391 days from August 20, 2000 to August 20, 2004.

On August 20, 2004, the applicant filed an application for citizenship in which he reported that he had been outside Canada for 391 days during the four years preceding the application, namely from August 20, 2000 to August 20, 2004.
The applicant met with a citizenship officer on February 27, 2006, stated he had been working abroad since the end of 2003, and filled out a questionnaire on residence.

On February 27, 2006, the applicant met with a citizenship officer. He stated that he had been working abroad since the end of 2003 and was asked to fill out a questionnaire on residence. the applicant filled out the questionnaire and sent it to the Department of Citizenship and Immigration on March 2, 2006.
The applicant attached documents to the questionnaire, including an explanatory letter stating 351 days of absence, family documents, and financial records.

A number of documents were attached to the questionnaire: an explanatory letter in which the applicant stated that he had been absent from Canada for 351 days during the period in question; various documents concerning the applicant’s wife and children; and other documents more directly connected with his situation (copy of his passport, termination of employment documents from…
The officer referred the file to a Citizenship Judge because the officer was not satisfied the documents showed significant presence in Canada.

On July 18, 2006, a Department officer referred the applicant’s file to a Citizenship Judge because the officer was not satisfied that the documents submitted showed a significant presence in Canada during the reference period. On July 10, 2008, the applicant was summoned to an interview with the Citizenship Judge, which was held on July 30, 2008. On August 1, 2008, the Citizen…
The Citizenship Judge was not satisfied with the evidence of residence and concluded the applicant did not meet paragraph 5(1)(c) of the Citizenship Act.

In the letter he sent the applicant on September 9, 2009, the Citizenship Judge informed him that he was not satisfied with the evidence submitted to establish the applicant’s residence in Canada and concluded that he therefore did not meet the requirements of paragraph 5(1)(c) of the Citizenship Act.
The Court notes the Citizenship Judge's reasons are set out in the notice sent to the Minister on July 30, 2009.
However, the reasons for his decision are set out more explicitly in the notice of the decision that the Citizenship Judge sent the Minister on July 30, 2009 (Court Record, pp. 9-11).
The Judge notes the applicant admits to being outside Canada for 391 days, meaning he does not meet the strict criterion of mandatory physical presence for 1095 days.

After identifying the relevant period as running from August 20, 2000 to August 20, 2004, the Judge notes that the applicant discloses that he was outside Canada for 391 days during that period. It is therefore clear that the applicant does not meet the strict criterion of mandatory physical presence for 1095 days during the period in issue, as the applicant himself admits.

The Judge was not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the applicant was physically present in Canada, citing unclear absence records, insufficient passport stamps, unsubstantiated occupation and community involvement, and incomplete or contradictory bank and credit card statements.

Moreover, the Judge indicates that after examining the documents provided by the applicant, he is not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the applicant was actually physically present in Canada during the number of days alleged. He then lists several reasons leading him to doubt the presence of the applicant in Canada: - The information provided by the applicant regard…
The Judge concluded on a balance of probabilities that the applicant was not physically present in Canada for the claimed days, noting the applicant declined to provide new evidence.

Given the evidence and the onus on the applicant to show that he met the residence requirements set out in paragraph 5(1)(c) of the Citizenship Act, the Judge therefore concluded, on a balance of probabilities, that the applicant was not physically present in Canada even during the 1069 days when he claimed to have been. It should be noted that the Judge says that he gave the a…
The only issue is whether the Citizenship Judge erred in denying the application because the applicant failed to meet the residence requirements of paragraph 5(1)(c) of the Citizenship Act.

The only issue in this application for judicial review is whether the Citizenship Judge erred in denying the applicant's application for citizenship on the ground that he failed to meet the requirements of paragraph 5(1)(c) of the Citizenship Act.
The standard of review for Citizenship Judges is reasonableness; the Court must show deference and not substitute its own view if the decision is intelligible, justified, and defensible.

It is now settled law that the standard of review applicable to the decisions of Citizenship Judges is that of reasonableness: see, for example, Zhang v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2008 FC 483; Chen v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FC 1140. Whether dealing with questions of mixed fact and law, as when applying one of the jurisprudential tests of the conc…
The applicant argues the Citizenship Judge erred by relying on the application form's 391 days of absence instead of the questionnaire's 351 days, claiming the discrepancy was a calculation error.

The applicant essentially faults the Citizenship Judge for not taking into account his residence questionnaire, in which he reported 351 days of absence, and for instead relying solely on his citizenship application form, in which he incorrectly reported 391 days of absence. The applicant argues that this total of 391 days was clearly the result of a calculation error, which hi…

The Court finds confusion in the applicant's record, noting that the periods of absence in his residence questionnaire do not match those in his citizenship application, so the discrepancies are more than mere calculation errors.

There is indeed a great deal of confusion in the applicant’s record having regard to his absences from Canada. In his initial citizenship application, it appears that the applicant did in fact make an error in computing his days of absence. Nevertheless, it is difficult to conclude that this was solely a calculation error, since the periods of absence entered in his residence q…
The Court finds the Citizenship Judge had difficulty determining the number of days of absence reported by the applicant, as the figures in the forms did not match the Judge's count.

The Citizenship Judge himself seems to have had difficulty determining with precision the number of days of absence reported by the applicant. In his notice to the Minister, the Judge counted a total of 10 absences for a total of 391 days, without really explaining how he arrived at that result. Yet even by combining the absences reported in the citizenship application with tho…
The Court finds the discrepancies are not fatal; the Judge denied the application because the applicant failed to demonstrate he was actually in Canada during unreported periods.

These discrepancies do not strike me as fatal, however, and probably reflect the confusion caused by the different versions provided by the applicant as to his absences from the country. The Judge ultimately denied the application for citizenship by relying not so much on the fact that the applicant had not accumulated the number of days required under paragraph 5(1)(c) of the …

The Court quotes section 5(1)(c) of the Citizenship Act, which requires a permanent resident to have accumulated at least three years of residence in Canada within the four years preceding the application.

Paragraph 5(1)(c) of the Citizenship Act reads as follows: Grant of citizenship 5. (1) The Minister shall grant citizenship to any person who (a) … (b) … (c) is a permanent resident within the meaning of subsection 2(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, and has, within the four years immediately preceding the date of his or her application, accumulated at least thr…
The Court notes it has consistently held a Citizenship Judge may apply three tests, including a strict day-count of actual physical presence, which was the approach taken by the Judge in this case.

However, this Court has consistently held that the Citizenship Judge can apply any of three tests to interpret the concept of residence: see, for example, Mizani v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FC 698. One of those tests consists in determining whether an applicant has been actually, physically present in Canada for a total of three years, calculated on the basis …
The Court finds the Judge cannot rely on the applicant's claims alone but must verify actual presence, as the applicant bears the burden of proving residence.

In applying this test, the Judge cannot rely on the applicant’s claims alone. He must also verify the applicant’s actual presence in Canada during the periods when the applicant claims that he was not outside the country. Accepting the applicant’s argument that the Judge erred by failing to accept the statements made by the applicant in his residence questionnaire would amount …
The Court finds the Judge was not satisfied by the documents that the applicant was physically present in Canada and committed no error in assessing the evidence.

In his analysis, the Judge examined the documents submitted by the applicant, which however did not satisfy him that the applicant had actually been physically present in Canada during the various periods as alleged. I have not been convinced that the Judge committed an error in assessing the evidence.

The Court notes the documents regarding the applicant's family proved nothing about his presence, bank records covered only short periods, and the Judge had reason to be astonished by the unsupported claim of setting up a corporation.

Thus, the documents concerning the applicant’s wife and children proved nothing with regard to the applicant’s presence in Canada. As for the documents concerning bank transactions, they covered only extremely short periods of time. Lastly, the Judge had reason to be astonished at the applicant’s claim that he had set up a corporation, when he adduced no document in support of …
The Court finds the Judge could legitimately doubt the applicant's physical presence, especially since the applicant turned down the opportunity to submit new documents.

In the absence of convincing evidence, the Judge could legitimately doubt the applicant’s physical presence in Canada during the period in issue. All the more so since the Judge says that he gave the applicant the opportunity to submit new documents during the interview, an offer which the applicant turned down.

The Court finds the Judge did not err and could reasonably conclude the applicant did not meet the residence requirements; the applicant has not satisfied the Court that the decision fell outside a range of acceptable outcomes.

Given the evidence in the record, I therefore find that the Citizenship Judge did not err and could reasonably conclude that the applicant did not meet the residence requirements under paragraph 5(1)(c) of the Citizenship Act. I understand the applicant’s disappointment, but he has not satisfied me that the decision of the Citizenship Judge did not fall within a range of possible, ac…

passes.title: Case at a glance
passes.what: Parties, how the case got here, subject, issues and each side's main arguments, in one card.
passes.where: Live in the Experimental reader for about 100 decisions.
passes.number_label: parties 90%, subject and issues 100%, challenged part 83%, true arguments found 93% (151 of 162)
passes.sample: 29 scored recent immigration decisions, none used for tuning.
passes.grader: Read by Haiku, graded by Sonnet (models, not lawyers).
passes.caveat: Small sample, and the grader was more lenient than in earlier rounds, so treat the figures as a few points optimistic.

passes.title: Issue map
passes.what: Each question the court decided, how it answered, and a jump to the paragraph that says so, with a "Check this" flag when the result is less certain.
passes.where: Built for the core 150 decisions; live in Experimental.
passes.number_label: result right and cited paragraph right
passes.sample: 152 decisions graded, about 95% on both counts.
passes.grader: Maps written by a free local model (Qwen3.5-9B); graded blind by Haiku.
passes.caveat: A few maps read the direction the wrong way round or marked a decided issue as undecided (3 decisions among the graded sets). Issues the grader never saw are not measured.

passes.what: One plain sentence on what each paragraph does, starting with who is speaking.
passes.where: Built for the core 150 decisions; shown in the Experimental reader.
passes.number_label: faithful, 0 wrong speaker, states the legal test in 94%
passes.grader: Written by a hosted open model, graded blind by Haiku.
passes.caveat: Soft qualifiers such as “partially” or “at most” are dropped in about 14% of notes. The notes name people by role (applicant, officer) rather than by name.

passes.title: Whose argument is this paragraph?
passes.what: Tags each paragraph with who is speaking: the applicant, the respondent, an earlier decision-maker or the judge.
passes.where: Stored for 39,617 decisions (live database count, 11 Oct 2026). Shown only above a confidence bar; the rest say Unsure.
passes.number_label: matches the stored labels (86% where a tag is shown)
passes.sample: 4,171 held-out paragraphs from 122 immigration decisions. Two model readers agreed on the speaker for 93.1% of 1,067 paragraphs.
passes.grader: Rules plus a small trained tagger, checked against model-written labels.
passes.caveat: The Refugee Protection Division is the weakest; no lawyer has reviewed these labels.

passes.title: Outline of a decision
passes.what: Splits a decision into units (facts, issues, reasoning, disposition) from its structure and headings.
passes.where: On the site today for decisions that have usable structure.
passes.number_label: right role for a unit (50% of unit boundaries exactly right)
passes.grader: Scored against hand-labelled sets, once, with no tuning.
passes.caveat: Exact boundaries are the hard part; the role is usually right even when the edge is a paragraph out. A small learned step added to the rules reached about 85% right role per paragraph on 47 hand-labelled decisions (about 90% for facts, reasoning and disposition). Finding where the analysis starts is only 55% within one paragraph. The labels themselves disagree, so about 92% is the practical ceiling.

passes.title: Find decided issues
passes.what: Given an argument, find earlier issues the courts have already decided.
passes.where: Experimental; the library holds 3,083 decided issues so far.
passes.number_label: a useful earlier issue in the top three (40 of 60 arguments)
passes.sample: 60 fresh arguments against the 3,083 decided issues, by word match.
passes.grader: Judged by a model, not a lawyer.
passes.caveat: Small sample. Matching your own draft is not built; nothing here reads or stores a draft.

passes.title: Outcome reading
passes.what: Reads who won from the ruling text with fixed rules, no AI. It says nothing when unsure.
passes.where: On the site today; shown on results and the reader.
passes.number_label: right when it gives an answer (4.5% are left blank)
passes.sample: 312 fresh decisions across two blind samples, before any tuning.
passes.grader: Checked against the ruling text; not reviewed by a lawyer.
passes.caveat: Mixed results in multi-appellant decisions and Supreme Court cross-appeals are left blank rather than guessed.

passes.title: Quick summaries
passes.what: A short summary built only from stored evidence, with the exact passage quoted. No AI at the time you read.
passes.sample: No accuracy figure has been measured yet.
passes.caveat: Until it is measured, treat it as a convenience, not a finding.

passes.title: Better citation links
passes.what: Finding every citation, including short forms such as “at para 44”, and resolving each to the right case and paragraph.
passes.where: New rules are written and tested on a first batch; the live site still uses the older rules.
passes.sample: A full rebuild and a before-and-after comparison on real cases come before the switch-over.
passes.caveat: No accuracy figure for the new rules yet.

limits: Every figure on this page was graded by a model on a small sample. No lawyer has reviewed them.
Paragraph notes and issue maps exist for a hand-picked set of about 150 important Federal Court decisions, not the whole library.
Reading your own draft against all this is planned. Nothing on this page reads or stores a draft.
Layout and wording are for review. This page is a picture built from real stored outputs, not the working feature.

helps.title: Where this helps in hearings and litigation work
helps.text: Five everyday jobs, each tied to the part that does it and to the evidence for it. The label beside each job says how far that part has got.

items.job: Get the point of a long decision before reading it in full
items.how: A case summary and a map of the questions the court decided, each with a link to the paragraph that decided it.

items.job: See whose argument a paragraph is dealing with
items.how: Each paragraph is tagged with the party or decision maker whose position it addresses, and you can filter by it.

items.job: Check how a cited case actually ended
items.how: The outcome is read from the ruling text, with the quoted sentence beside it. Unclear cases are left blank, not guessed.

items.job: Find earlier decisions on the same question
items.how: Given an argument, finds decided issues from earlier Federal Court decisions. Matching your own draft is not built.

items.job: Cite to the right paragraph every time
items.how: Short forms such as “at para 44” resolve to the right case and paragraph. This is the least measured part.
